name: Janakpur
tagline: Sita's city, white marble and two hundred sacred ponds
meta_description: Janakpur, capital of Mithila in Nepal: Janaki Mandir, Vivah Mandap, Ganga Sagar and Dhanush Sagar, Mithila painting, Nepal's railway and how to get there.
summary: Janakpur, or Janakpurdham, is the capital of Madhesh Province and the heart of Nepal's Mithila. Hindus honour it as the home of Sita and the place of her wedding to Rama. See the white Janaki Mandir, finished in 1910 to 1911, the wedding pavilion, sacred ponds and Mithila painting by local women. Give it one or two days, October to March.
intro: Janakpur is unlike anywhere else on a Nepal itinerary. It lies on the hot, flat Mithila plain about 225 km south-east of Kathmandu, a city of cycle rickshaws, bright saris, temple bells and more than 200 sacred ponds. Maithili is the language of the street, and the city is the cultural centre of Nepal's Maithil people. The city is flat, hot for much of the year and easy to explore by cycle rickshaw.

At its heart stands the Janaki Mandir, a three-storey palace-temple of white stone and marble dedicated to Sita, also known as Janaki, daughter of King Janaka. Pilgrims from across Nepal and India come to worship here and at the neighbouring Vivah Mandap, the pavilion that marks the wedding of Rama and Sita described in the Ramayana. Pilgrims arrive by bus, train and plane, and the temple courtyard is busy from early morning until late evening.

We recommend Janakpur to travellers who want to see the Terai's devotional life and its art. Women here have painted the walls of their homes in the Mithila style for generations, and today they also paint on paper and fabric. Fly in from Kathmandu in about half an hour, spend a full day in the old centre, and add Dhanusha Dham if you have a second day. October to March is the comfortable season.

story.title: A pilgrim town built around a story
paras: Hindus have long identified this part of Mithila with Videha, the kingdom of King Janaka in the Ramayana, and with the birthplace of Sita. The modern city, though, is younger than the legend. Accounts from priests and bards suggest Janakpur grew as a cluster of monasteries and hamlets in the 18th century, and the first written description of it as a pilgrimage site dates from 1805. Its founder is remembered as the ascetic saint Sannyasi Shurkishordas. The legend came first; the city grew to honour it.

The defining building came at the start of the 20th century. Queen Vrisha Bhanu of Tikamgarh, in the Orchha state of central India, funded a grand temple to Sita, completed in 1910 to 1911. It cost so much, nine lakh by tradition, that people still call it the Nau Lakha Mandir. Its domes, small towers, lattice windows and 60 rooms make it unlike any other temple in Nepal, and it was placed on Nepal's UNESCO tentative list in 2008. Parts of the temple were damaged in the April 2015 earthquake.

After the Sugauli Treaty of 1816 drew the border through Mithila, Janakpur stayed in Nepal while most of the region went to British India. The city grew into a market town, gained Nepal's only railway in the 1930s and is now the capital of Madhesh Province. Ayodhya and Janakpur became sister cities in 2014, a link pilgrims celebrate each year at Vivaha Panchami. Today Janakpur is a crowded, growing city, but its ponds, temples and festivals keep the old rhythm of pilgrimage at its centre.

legend: In the Ramayana, King Janaka found the infant Sita in a furrow while ploughing. When she grew up, he declared that only a man who could string Shiva's great bow could marry her. Princes failed one after another; Rama lifted the bow and broke it. Local tradition says a golden image of Sita was found at the site of the Janaki Mandir in 1657, which is why the temple stands here.
people: Janakpur is a Maithil city. Most residents speak Maithili, with Nepali and Hindi also common. Brahmin and Kayastha families have long served as priests and scholars, while Yadav, Teli, Kushwaha, Muslim and Dalit families work as farmers, traders and artisans. Maithil women keep alive the painting traditions of kohbar and aripan, now also a source of income.

untold.fact: Janaki Mandir is also called the Nau Lakha Mandir, nine lakh temple, after the cost of its construction; Queen Vrisha Bhanu of Tikamgarh completed it in 1910 to 1911.
Janakpur has more than 200 sacred ponds used for ritual bathing; the two most important, Dhanush Sagar and Ganga Sagar, lie close to the city centre.
Ayodhya, honoured as Rama's birthplace, and Janakpur, honoured as Sita's, became sister cities in November 2014.

taste.name: Machh-bhaat
taste.text: Fish and rice is the soul of Maithil food: freshwater fish from local ponds, cooked in mustard oil and mustard paste with turmeric and chilli, eaten with plain rice. Maithils even list fish among the marks of Mithila. Try it at local eateries near the market, or ask your guide for a home-cooked meal.

facts: ≈ 225 km · 6–8 h by road; 25–30 min by air

highlights.title: Janaki Mandir
highlights.text: The white marble temple to Sita, completed in 1910 to 1911, with domes, towers and lattice windows. Come in the evening, when lamps are lit and bells and singing fill the courtyard. Remove shoes at the gate.

highlights.title: Vivah Mandap
highlights.text: Beside the temple, a pavilion marks the wedding of Rama and Sita, with figures of the wedding party. It is the focus of the Vivaha Panchami festival in late November or December. Pilgrims crowd it on festival days.

highlights.title: Ganga Sagar and Dhanush Sagar
highlights.text: Janakpur's two most sacred ponds, near the centre, are lined with ghats and temples. At dawn people bathe, wash clothes and pray; at Chhath they fill with offerings. Dawn is the best time to visit.

highlights.title: Mithila painting
highlights.text: Maithil women paint bold, colourful scenes of gods, weddings, fish, birds and daily life. Visit a women's art centre near the city to watch artists at work and buy directly from them. Buying direct supports the painters.

highlights.title: Nepal's only railway
highlights.text: Janakpur is the hub of Nepal Railways, running trains toward Jaynagar in Bihar. A short ride shows the flat Mithila countryside from a slow carriage window. Check timetables the day before, as services change.

how_to_reach.text: Several daily flights connect Kathmandu with Janakpur Airport (JKR) in about 25 to 30 minutes. The airport is in the city, a few minutes by car or rickshaw from the Janaki Mandir. Check current status before you travel.

By road it is about 225 km and 6 to 8 hours from Kathmandu via the BP Highway through Dhulikhel, Sindhuli and Bardibas. Night and day buses run from Kathmandu. From Chitwan allow 7 to 8 hours via Hetauda and the East-West Highway.

where_to_stay: Janakpur has simple to mid-range city hotels, most within a short rickshaw ride of the Janaki Mandir and the ponds. Comforts are modest compared with Kathmandu or Chitwan: choose a hotel with air conditioning from March to October and ask for a room away from the main road. Rooms fill fast for Vivaha Panchami, Chhath and Rama Navami, so book weeks ahead. There are no international chain hotels.
tips: Visit the Janaki Mandir twice: early morning for quiet, evening for lamps and music.
Dress modestly, remove shoes at temples and ask before photographing worshippers.
Use cycle rickshaws or e-rickshaws to move between the temple, ponds and markets; agree the fare first.
Buy Mithila paintings directly from women's art centres so the money goes to the artists.
Avoid April to June, when temperatures on the plain often pass 40 °C.

experiences.title: Evening at the Janaki Mandir
experiences.summary: Visit the white marble temple to Sita at dusk, when lamps are lit, bells ring and devotees sing in the courtyard, then walk across to the Vivah Mandap, the pavilion that marks Sita's wedding to Rama.
body: The Janaki Mandir rises from a large courtyard in the centre of Janakpur, all white stone and marble, with domes, small towers and lattice windows. It covers about 1,480 square metres and holds 60 rooms. In the inner sanctum a flower-covered image of Sita stands with Rama and his brothers. Inside, walls carry Mithila paintings, and the courtyard holds thousands of people on festival days.

Come in the late afternoon and stay until dark. As the light fades, priests light lamps, bells ring and devotional songs begin. Families arrive in their best clothes, newlyweds come to seek blessings and pilgrims from India sit in groups on the marble floor. The atmosphere is warm, busy and moving. Musicians play harmonium and cymbals, and devotees sing bhajans in Maithili and Hindi.

Afterwards, walk to the Vivah Mandap next door, a pavilion with figures depicting the wedding of Rama and Sita. Remove shoes at the gate, cover shoulders and knees, keep phones on silent and ask before photographing people at prayer. Rickshaws wait outside the gate for the ride back to your hotel. Allow about two hours and carry a small torch for the lanes.

faqs.q: When was the Janaki Mandir built?
faqs.a: The Janaki Mandir was built by Queen Vrisha Bhanu of Tikamgarh, in the Orchha state of central India, and completed in 1910 to 1911. It is known as the Nau Lakha Mandir after its legendary cost of nine lakh. It was placed on Nepal's UNESCO tentative list in 2008.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus enter the Janaki Mandir?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors of all faiths are welcome in the temple courtyard and most public areas. Remove shoes, dress modestly and behave quietly. Photography rules inside the inner sanctum may be restricted; follow signs and ask staff. Staff are used to foreign visitors.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Janaki Mandir?
faqs.a: Early morning for quiet and soft light, and dusk for the evening rituals with lamps, bells and singing. Festival days such as Vivaha Panchami and Rama Navami are spectacular but very crowded. From April to June midday heat is intense, so visit early or late.

experiences.title: Mithila painting with women artists
experiences.summary: Visit a women's art centre near Janakpur to watch Maithil women paint gods, weddings, fish and peacocks in bold colour, learn the meaning of kohbar and aripan, and try a simple design yourself. Buying direct supports the artists.
body: Mithila painting, known in India as Madhubani art, has been made by women in this region for generations. It began on freshly plastered mud walls and floors for weddings, births and festivals: the kohbar painted in the wedding chamber, the aripan drawn in rice paste on the floor before a ritual. Mothers taught daughters, and designs passed down through families.

Around Janakpur, women's art centres and cooperatives now train painters to work on paper, cloth and pottery as well as walls. A visit lets you watch artists at work, see how they build a design from outlines and fill it with dense patterns, and hear what the symbols mean: fish for fertility, bamboo and lotus for the couple, sun and moon for long life. Each centre and each painter has a recognisable style.

Many centres let visitors try a small design with a bamboo pen or brush. Pieces for sale range from postcards to large panels; buying directly supports the artists. Ask your guide to arrange the visit, especially on public holidays when some centres close. Many centres also sell cushion covers, bags and pottery decorated with Mithila designs, which are easier to carry home than framed paintings.

faqs.q: What is Mithila painting?
faqs.a: Mithila painting is a folk art of the Mithila region of Nepal and India, traditionally made by women on house walls and floors for weddings, festivals and rituals. It uses bold outlines, bright colours and dense patterns to show gods, wedding scenes, animals and nature. In India it is often called Madhubani art.

faqs.q: Where can I see Mithila painting in Janakpur?
faqs.a: You can see it on house walls in villages around Janakpur, especially near festivals and weddings, and at women's art centres and cooperatives near the city, where artists paint on paper, cloth and pottery. The Janaki Mandir and some public buildings also have painted walls.

faqs.q: How much does a Mithila painting cost?
faqs.a: Small paintings and cards are inexpensive, a few hundred Nepali rupees, while large, detailed works on paper or cloth cost much more. Prices depend on size, detail and the artist. Buying from women's centres or directly from artists ensures they receive a fair share.

experiences.title: Sacred ponds and the Ram Mandir at dawn
experiences.summary: Walk Janakpur's old centre at dawn, from Ganga Sagar to Dhanush Sagar, as people bathe, pray and wash on the ghats, then visit the pagoda-style Ram Mandir that faces Dhanush Sagar. Go early for the soft light.
body: Janakpur is known as a city of ponds, with more than 200 used for bathing and ritual. The most sacred, Ganga Sagar and Dhanush Sagar, lie close together near the centre. At dawn the ghats fill with people: men bathing and offering water to the sun, women in bright saris, priests setting out flowers and vermilion. Small shrines stand at the water's edge.

Between the ponds stands the Ram Mandir, one of the oldest temples in the city, first built in the 17th century and rebuilt later in a Nepali pagoda style unusual on the plains. It faces Dhanush Sagar, and within its complex is a shrine known as Rajdevi Mandir. It is busiest at Rama Navami in spring, the festival of Rama's birth.

Walk slowly through the lanes between the ponds, where tea stalls open, flower sellers string marigolds and rickshaw drivers wait for the first passengers. The light is soft and the city at its quietest. Ask before taking photographs of people bathing. Allow two to three hours, and end with tea and breakfast at a stall near the Janaki Mandir.

faqs.q: How many ponds are there in Janakpur?
faqs.a: Janakpur has more than 200 sacred ponds used for ritual bathing, along with many smaller ones. The two most important are Ganga Sagar and Dhanush Sagar, close to the city centre. Many are linked to stories from the Ramayana and to festivals such as Chhath.

faqs.q: Who built the Ram Mandir in Janakpur?
faqs.a: The Ram Mandir was first built in the 17th century by Chaturbhuj Giri and later rebuilt in a Nepali pagoda style. It stands directly in front of Dhanush Sagar pond, a short walk from the Janaki Mandir, and contains a shrine called Rajdevi Mandir.

faqs.q: Can I swim in the ponds of Janakpur?
faqs.a: The ponds are sacred and used for ritual bathing and prayer, not for swimming. Visitors are welcome to watch from the ghats. Water quality varies, so we do not recommend entering the water. Ask before photographing people bathing. Respect the bathers' privacy.

experiences.title: Ride Nepal's only passenger railway
experiences.summary: Take a short ride on Nepal Railways from Janakpur across the Mithila plain, past rice fields, ponds and villages, on the country's only working passenger line, which runs toward Jaynagar in Bihar. Check the timetable first.
body: Nepal has only one working passenger railway, and it starts in Janakpur. The line runs south-east across the Mithila plain toward Jaynagar in Bihar, about 52 km from the border at Jaynagar to Bhangaha in Nepal. A narrow-gauge line first ran here in the 1930s; it was rebuilt to broad gauge and reopened in the 2020s. The station is a short rickshaw ride from the centre.

A short ride from Janakpur station toward one of the nearby stops, then back by road, is a fun half day. From the window you see the flat, green plain at walking pace: ponds full of buffalo, mango orchards, mud-walled villages and children waving from the fields. Carriages are busy with traders, students and families. Tickets are cheap and sold at the station.

Timetables change and services are sometimes suspended, so check the day before at the station or with your guide. Foreign travellers should not ride across the border unless the crossing is approved for third-country nationals and they hold a valid Indian visa. Allow two to three hours for a short ride and return, and bring water and small notes for snacks sold on the platform.

faqs.q: Does Nepal have a railway?
faqs.a: Yes. Nepal Railways runs the country's only passenger service, on the line linking Jaynagar in Bihar with Janakpur and stations further into Nepal. A railway first ran here in the 1930s; the line was converted to broad gauge and services resumed in the 2020s. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners ride the Janakpur train?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors can ride within Nepal, between Janakpur and nearby stations. Crossing into India by train is only allowed where the border point is open to third-country nationals, with a valid visa. Ask at Janakpur station or check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long is the train ride from Janakpur?
faqs.a: A short ride to a nearby station takes under an hour, and many visitors return by road. The full journey to Jaynagar on the Indian side takes about two hours depending on stops. Schedules change, so confirm times at the station the day before.

faqs.q: Why is Janakpur famous?
faqs.a: Janakpur is honoured by Hindus as the home of Sita, daughter of King Janaka, and the place of her wedding to Rama in the Ramayana. It is famous for the white marble Janaki Mandir, completed in 1910 to 1911, its many sacred ponds, Mithila painting and festivals such as Vivaha Panchami and Chhath.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kathmandu to Janakpur?
faqs.a: Fly from Kathmandu to Janakpur in about 25 to 30 minutes; several flights run daily. By road it is about 225 km and 6 to 8 hours via the BP Highway through Sindhuli and Bardibas. Overnight and day buses run from Kathmandu.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Janakpur?
faqs.a: One full day covers the Janaki Mandir, Vivah Mandap, Ram Mandir, the main ponds and a Mithila art centre. A second day lets you visit Dhanusha Dham, ride the railway and see village life. Add extra days if you come for a festival.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Janakpur?
faqs.a: October to March. Late October to mid-November brings Chhath, and late November or December brings Vivaha Panchami. January can be foggy and cool. April to June is extremely hot, often over 40 °C, and the monsoon from late June brings heavy rain.

faqs.q: Is Janakpur safe for tourists?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Janakpur is a busy pilgrim city used to visitors from India and across Nepal. Take normal precautions with valuables in crowds, especially during festivals. Political strikes occasionally close roads and shops in Madhesh; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What language is spoken in Janakpur?
faqs.a: Maithili is the main language of Janakpur and the surrounding area. Nepali and Hindi are widely understood, and hotel and temple staff often speak some English. Learning a greeting such as pranam is appreciated. Hotel staff can help with directions.

faqs.q: What should I wear in Janakpur?
faqs.a: Light, loose clothes that cover shoulders and knees, especially for temple visits. Women may want a scarf to cover their head in some shrines. Shoes come off at temple gates, so slip-on sandals are practical. Bring a hat and sunscreen, and a warm layer for winter evenings.

faqs.q: Can I combine Janakpur with Chitwan?
faqs.a: Yes, but distances are long by road, about 7 to 8 hours. Most travellers fly Kathmandu–Janakpur and Kathmandu–Bharatpur separately, or drive the East-West Highway with a night's stop. A combined trip of eight to ten nights can include Chitwan, Janakpur and Koshi Tappu.

faqs.q: Where can I buy Mithila paintings in Janakpur?
faqs.a: At women's art centres and cooperatives near Janakpur, at shops around the Janaki Mandir and directly from artists in nearby villages. Buying from women's centres or artists gives them a fairer share. Ask your guide to arrange a visit to watch painters at work before you buy.
